items.title: Is meaningful privacy possible with hosted AI models?
items.raw_excerpt: I've been thinking about the privacy tradeoffs when using frontier AI models like Claude or chatgpt. Even with a VPN, providers still see prompts, and usage is tied to accounts and payment methods linked to identity in some way. I've been trying to find a way to access these models without creating provider-specific accounts tied to my identity. Ideally, through some kind of intermediary that abstracts identity and doesn't retain prompts. From a technical and economic perspective, would that kind of setup meaningfully improve privacy, or does it just shift trust? Is meaningful privacy with hosted AI fundamentally unrealistic regardless of architecture?

items.title: AI-runtime-guard – Policy enforcement layer for MCP AI agents
items.raw_excerpt:
I built this after realizing that AI agents with filesystem and shell access can delete files, leak credentials, or execute destructive commands — and there's no enforcement layer stopping them at the execution level. ai-runtime-guard is an MCP server that sits between your AI agent and your system. It enforces a policy layer before any file or shell action takes effect. No retraining, no prompt engineering, no changes to your agent or workflow. Your agent can say anything. It can only do what policy allows. What it does:
- Blocks dangerous commands (rm -rf, dd, shutdown, privilege escalation) before execution
- Gates risky commands behind human approval via a web GUI
- Simulates blast radius for wildcard operations before they run
- Creates automatic backups before destructive actions

However, it then suffered a cliff-like decline. As of the time of writing, the stock price has fallen by over 50% from its peak, with its market capitalization similarly halved. Oracle, which has clearly anchored its transformation direction in cloud + AI infrastructure and precisely caught the core wave of AI computing demand, why did its soaring stock price suddenly brake sharply? excerpt_i18n.es: El juego de Oracle como "revendedor de IA" parece estar llegando a su fin. A principios de este mes, un rumor sobre despidos de 30.000 empleados expuso completamente las dificultades financieras de Oracle. Según un informe de análisis especializado publicado por TD Cowen, debido a problemas de financiación en la expansión de centros de datos de IA, Oracle enfrenta una severa presión financiera y está considerando despedir entre 20.000 y 30.000 empleados en el corto plazo para liberar un flujo de efectivo de 8.000 a 10.000 millones de dólares. Esta presión operativa ya se refleja claramente en la tendencia del precio de sus acciones. En el último año, este gigante tecnológico con más de 40 años de experiencia ha protagonizado una emocionante "montaña rusa" en su cotización: un aumento escalonado a principios de año, seguido de una caída del 35% en un solo día el 10 de septiembre.

Author: Hu Jiaming  Editors: Dong Zibo, Lin Juemin  
On the afternoon of February 2, independent developer and founder of AI gaming company AutoGame, Zhang Haoyang, received a startling email that read: "If you donate $1,000 to this project, we will investigate this matter for you now."  
It all began with Zhang Haoyang’s plugin "Capability Evolver," which he published on OpenClaw. Having just started using OpenClaw two days prior, Zhang had manually developed a self-evolving engine for AI Agents. It could identify improvements in Agents and enable them to break through the limitations of "local optima" through random "mutations."  
Within less than a day of its release on Clawhub, the plugin’s core code garnered over 17,000 downloads and consistently ranked first on the platform’s trending chart.  
However, a day later, the plugin was inexplicably and suddenly removed from the platform.  
After the plugin was taken down, Zhang Haoyang emailed OpenClaw’s author, Peter Steinberger, to inquire about the reason for the removal and how to cooperate to have the plugin reinstated.  
The official response, however, was the "bribery letter" mentioned at the beginning of the article—which truly shocked Zhang Haoyang.

excerpt_i18n.en: In the development of medical artificial intelligence, evaluation methods have largely shaped the direction of technological evolution. For a considerable period, progress in medical AI primarily revolved around the acquisition and reasoning of medical knowledge, with models' "intelligence" often measured by static benchmarks such as medical exam questions and clinical Q&A datasets. Under this evaluation framework, models were considered to possess high medical capability as long as they provided correct answers under conditions of complete information and closed questions. With the rise of large language models, this approach quickly achieved breakthroughs, with multiple systems reaching or surpassing human expert levels in tests like MedQA, leading to optimistic industry assessments about whether "medical AI has matured." However, as these models were gradually introduced into interactive scenarios closer to real clinical practice, a long-overlooked issue emerged: real medical practice is not about making diagnoses based on complete information but a dynamic process of gradually approaching decisions through continuous questioning, risk identification, and information integration under conditions of high uncertainty. The knowledge advantages demonstrated by models in static evaluations did not naturally translate into reliable support for real consultation scenarios; instead, they exposed flaws in multi-turn dialogues, such as rigid questioning strategies, slow responses to high-risk signals, premature conclusions, and a lack of basic communication and empathy.
